_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 7 Press, Shake, Clap. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: the device and its inputs and outputs (with the micro:bit beat the deepened lecture adds), the when block, the outputs one at a time, testing and debugging, computers controlling machines, and sense-decide-act. Bitsy's board is DRAWN here - the kit keeps it inside a closure and there is no ART.sim - but every light pattern comes from ART.leds, every block label and icon from ART.device.block, and the order the outputs run in from ART.device.plan, so no picture can disagree with the lesson.
title: Press, Shake, Clap
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Know how to create programs to produce an output from an input device.
Know how to develop programs for a physical computing device to produce outputs.
Know how to test and debug programs so that they run and produce the desired output.
Know that computers can be programmed to control machines and other physical objects.

beats.say: Press a button. Shake it. Clap your hands.
Bitsy is a small computer you can hold, and it feels all three.
Bitsy is a physical computing device: a small computer with real parts on it.
Button A is an input. Press it, and the program can feel it.
The shake sensor feels a shake. The microphone hears a clap.
Twenty-five little lights, a speaker, a motor and a bell are outputs.
Bitsy has no screen, but it runs programs. It is a computer.
The micro:bit is a real board with two buttons and a grid of lights.
A device program starts with a when block. It names the input.
When button A is pressed. That is the input this program waits for.
Then come the outputs: show a heart, beep.
Press A, and Bitsy draws a heart and beeps.
Shake it instead and nothing happens. The program is waiting for A.
Each output block makes Bitsy do one real thing.
All lights on turns every one of the twenty-five lights on.

at.every: every one of the twenty-five lights

beats.say: Show a smile draws a smile. All lights off makes them dark.
Beep uses the speaker. Turn the motor. Ring the bell.
When the input arrives, the outputs run in order, one after another.
The algorithm says show a heart. You pressed A and got a smile.

at.algorithm: The algorithm says show a heart

beats.say: Do not give up. Change the smile block for a heart block.
Press A again to test it. Now Bitsy shows a heart.
Testing a program and fixing it is called debugging.
If nothing happens at all, the when block has the wrong input.
A program is not only for screens. It moves real things too.
Through a motor or a switch, traffic lights change and a door opens.

at.motor: Through a motor or a switch

beats.say: A washing machine turns its drum. A lift climbs to the floor you pressed.

at.washing: A washing machine turns its drum

beats.say: Inside each one is a small computer following a program.
Every control system has the same three parts.
Something senses: a button, a sensor, a microphone.
Something decides: the program says what to do.

at.program: the program says what to do

beats.say: Something acts: a light, a motor, a speaker.
Try it on a shop door that opens as you walk up.
A press, a shake and a clap are inputs Bitsy can feel.
The when block goes first and names the input. Then the outputs run.
Test it, fix it, and a program can control a real machine.
